title: OpenAI Begins Testing 'Private Inference': Customer Data Isolated During Model Runtime, Even Internal Employees Cannot View It

content_html:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman announced today on X that the company has invited some customers to test its “Private Inference” feature. This is the latest feature in OpenAI’s Private Intelligence product line, mainly aimed at improving data privacy protection in workplace scenarios.

The core mechanism of “Private Inference” is to isolate customer data while the model is running. According to Kuai Technology, the feature achieves “zero-snooping”-level data isolation—even OpenAI internal employees cannot view customer data content when customers use Private Inference. This design addresses enterprise customers’ core concerns about data security and privacy compliance in AI services, especially in sensitive industries such as finance, healthcare, and law.

At present, the testing scope is limited to “a small number of customers,” and no timetable has been announced for a full rollout. Altman positions it as part of OpenAI Private Intelligence, indicating that OpenAI is evolving from general AI services to a tiered privacy architecture—free users, Plus users, enterprise users, and Private Inference users will be at different levels of data protection.

This move also comes against the backdrop of tightening AI privacy regulation. Previously, OpenAI sparked controversy over its data usage policies, including an August 2025 announcement that it would monitor user chats and report threatening content to police. The launch of Private Inference can be seen as a key step in OpenAI’s rebuilding of privacy trust—proving the effectiveness of data isolation through technical means rather than policy promises.

For enterprise customers, the value of Private Inference lies in being able to enjoy frontier model capabilities while meeting internal compliance requirements and external regulatory standards. If testing goes well, this feature could become a core selling point of OpenAI’s enterprise-grade services, and a bargaining chip to pull ahead of competitors such as Microsoft Azure OpenAI Service on the privacy dimension.
